summary: Specifies the Hop-Limit option for CoAP to prevent and detect infinite forwarding loops that proxies can cause. Each proxy decrements a counter so a request that goes around in circles eventually stops.

eli5.summary: A note with a number on it that goes down each time it is passed along. When it reaches zero, nobody passes it on anymore, so it cannot circle forever.

questions: how to prevent coap proxy loops
what is the coap hop-limit option
what is the default coap hop-limit value
subtitle: A counter that each CoAP proxy decrements, so a request stuck in a proxy loop is stopped and reported.

tldr.problem: When a CoAP request passes through several proxies, a routing misconfiguration or policy conflict can make it circle forever.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8768 adds a Hop-Limit option (number 16) that each understanding proxy decrements before forwarding, and a 5.08 (Hop Limit Reached) error that is returned when the counter runs out.
tldr.outcome: Loops are cut off and reported, with proxy identifiers in the error payload to help troubleshooting. New CoAP proxies MUST implement the option and have it enabled by default.

today: RFC 8768 is a Proposed Standard from March 2020. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: Proxy Loops
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) is used more and more as a communication protocol between application agents. The RFC gives one example: a signaling protocol between domains under distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack and their DDoS mitigation providers. A CoAP client can talk to a server directly or through one or more proxies.

When several proxies are involved, infinite forwarding loops can occur, for example through routing misconfiguration or policy conflicts. This document defines a new CoAP option, Hop-Limit, to prevent such loops, and a new response code to report them together with diagnostic information.

The intended usage is general, not limited to the original use case: new CoAP proxies MUST implement the option and have it enabled by default. A server that gets requests both directly and via proxies will see otherwise identical requests with and without the option, so servers with internal caching will also want to implement it to improve caching efficiency.
sections.eli5: If a message is handed from helper to helper and the helpers get confused, it could go around the same circle forever. This RFC gives the message a way to say when it has been passed along too many times.

sections.title: The Hop-Limit Option
sections.content:
Hop-Limit is CoAP option number 16. Its value is an unsigned integer of length 1. The default is 16. None of the Critical, Unsafe, NoCacheKey or Repeatable properties is marked for it, so it is an elective option and is not repeatable. A request carrying several Hop-Limit options MUST be handled as RFC 7252 describes for repeated options.

The value MUST be between 1 and 255 inclusive. A request received with the option set to 0 or to more than 255 MUST be rejected by the server or proxy with 4.00 (Bad Request).

The option is safe to forward, so a proxy that does not understand it should pass it on. It is also part of the cache key. Loops made up only of proxies that do not understand the option cannot be detected, but if at least one proxy in the loop supports it, the loop is still caught.
sections.eli5: The option is a small number on the request, from 1 to 255, and it starts at 16 if nobody picks another number. Helpers that do not know about the number just pass it along.

sections.title: How Proxies Handle the Counter
sections.content:
A proxy that understands the option SHOULD be instructed, by a configuration parameter, to insert a Hop-Limit option when it relays a request that does not have one. The initial value should be configurable. If no value is configured, the default of 16 MUST be used. The RFC explains the choice: in most cases it is large enough that a request is not dropped when there is no loop, but not so large that it wastes proxy resources when a loop does occur. Lower values should be used with caution and only where the topology is known.

Otherwise, a proxy that understands the option MUST decrement the value by 1 before forwarding. A request MUST NOT be forwarded if the value is 0 after the decrement. Such a request cannot be forwarded and SHOULD be logged, and a 5.08 (Hop Limit Reached) error response is sent back to the CoAP peer. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to support ways of alerting administrators about loop errors.

Caching has a rule of its own. A proxy MUST NOT use a stored 5.08 response unless the Hop-Limit in the new request is smaller than or equal to the one in the request that produced the stored response. The reason is that a request which failed with a given value will also fail with a smaller one.

Proxies at the boundary of an administrative domain MAY be instructed to remove or rewrite the received Hop-Limit value. This should be done with caution, because traffic that repeatedly crosses the boundary in a loop would make loop detection ineffective.
sections.eli5: Every helper subtracts one from the number before passing the message on. If the number hits zero, the helper stops, writes down what happened and sends back an error instead.

sections.title: Debugging With the 5.08 Response
sections.content:
To help troubleshooting, the proxy that detects a loop puts an identifier for itself in the diagnostic payload of the 5.08 (Hop Limit Reached) response. The identifier MUST NOT contain a space character. It can be a proxy name such as p11.example.net, an alias such as myproxyalias, or an IP address such as 2001:db8::1.

Each intermediate proxy that relays the 5.08 error prepends its own identifier to the diagnostic payload, using a space as separator, and only one identifier per proxy should appear. This keeps the message small and makes it easy to correlate with the hop count. A proxy prepends its identifier only if there is enough room according to the Path MTU. If not, it forwards the error without changing the payload.

An intermediate proxy MUST NOT forward a 5.08 error if it finds its own identifier already in the diagnostic payload. Such messages SHOULD be logged and alerts sent to administrators.
sections.eli5: When the message is stopped, each helper that passes the bad news back writes its name on it. Reading the list of names shows who was part of the circle.

sections.title: Mapping to HTTP
sections.content:
The RFC adds rules for proxies that translate between HTTP and CoAP. By default an HTTP-to-CoAP proxy inserts a Hop-Limit option following the rules above. Policy may instead tell it to insert the option only if a Via or CDN-Loop header field is present in the HTTP request.

The HTTP-to-CoAP proxy maps 5.08 (Hop Limit Reached) to the HTTP status 508 (Loop Detected), and the CoAP-to-HTTP proxy maps 508 back to 5.08. By default the CoAP-to-HTTP proxy inserts a Via header field in the HTTP request if the CoAP request had a Hop-Limit option, and policy may tell it to use CDN-Loop instead.

If traffic repeatedly crosses both kinds of proxy, loop detection may break. A loop that stays within the CoAP part or within the HTTP part is still detected.
sections.eli5: Some helpers translate between two languages. They also translate the stop signal, so a loop is noticed on either side of the translator.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered two entries in the CoAP parameter registries. In the CoAP Response Codes subregistry, code 5.08 is named Hop Limit Reached. In the CoAP Option Numbers subregistry, number 16 is named Hop-Limit. Both entries point to RFC 8768.
sections.eli5: The official list of CoAP numbers got two new lines: one for the new option and one for the new error.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues of CoAP proxying are covered in RFC 7252. This RFC adds two points.

First, a CoAP endpoint can probe the topology of a network by tweaking the Hop-Limit value. Such probing is likely to fail if proxies at the network boundary rewrite the value they receive.

Second, the diagnostic payload of a 5.08 response may reveal the topology of an administrative domain. A proxy at the boundary MAY be instructed to strip the payload, or part of it, before forwarding the response.
sections.eli5: Someone could change the number to learn how many helpers sit inside a network, and the list of names on an error could give away the layout. Helpers at the edge can hide these clues.
